Bewray
be-RAY
verb
From Middle English bewreyen, to accuse or disclose — the prefix be- joined to Old English wrēgan, to accuse or make known; not the same word as “betray,” though it drifts near it, meaning to reveal, expose, or give away.

Biblical Definition

To bewray is to disclose what was meant to be hidden — to let a thing out, whether by tongue, by trembling, or by the tell-tale accent of a man’s speech. The word can carry guilt or innocence in the same breath. The partner of a thief “heareth cursing, and bewrayeth it not” (Pro 29:24): his silence bewrays his heart, for the man who will not testify to a crime has joined it. In Isaiah the prophet pleads the opposite duty — “hide the outcasts; bewray not him that wandereth” (Isa 16:3) — where to bewray is to betray the fugitive to his hunters. But the word’s most piercing use is in the high priest’s courtyard, where a servant girl says to Peter, “Surely thou also art one of them; for thy speech bewrayeth thee” (Mat 26:73). His Galilean tongue disclosed what his oaths denied; the man could change his words but not his voice, and the voice preached the truth against him. Herein is the law of the mouth: what a man is will out, for “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh” (Mat 12:34). Sin is a poor secret-keeper. Grace, too, bewrays itself — the accent of heaven clings to the born-again man, and his speech, seasoned with salt, discloses whose he is before he means to confess it.

Webster 1828 Definition

To reveal or expose what was hidden — famously, Peter’s Galilean speech bewraying him in the high priest’s hall.

expand to see more

BEWRAY, to disclose, reveal, or expose; to make known what was concealed.

Distinct from “betray,” though it approaches it: to give a thing away.

“Thy speech bewrayeth thee” — Peter’s accent discloses him (Mat 26:73).

To bewray the wanderer (Isa 16:3) is to hand him to his pursuers.

What the heart hides, the mouth bewrays: the law of Matthew 12:34.

Key Scripture

Pro 29:24 — "Whoso is partner with a thief hateth his own soul: he heareth cursing, and bewrayeth it not."

Isa 16:3 — "Take counsel, execute judgment; make thy shadow as the night in the midst of the noonday; hide the outcasts; bewray not him that wandereth."

Mat 26:73 — "And after a while came unto him they that stood by, and said to Peter, Surely thou also art one of them; for thy speech bewrayeth thee."

Mat 12:34 — "O generation of vipers, how can ye, being evil, speak good things? for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh."

Modern Corruption

Not a contested doctrine but a lost verb; recovering it recovers the truth that what a man is will out, in his speech and his silence alike.

expand to see more

The temptation the word rebukes is the modern conceit that a man can curate himself — that the self is what we broadcast, not what leaks out under pressure. Scripture knows better. The heart bewrays itself in an unguarded accent, a nervous silence, a word spoken in anger; the mask slips in the courtyard when the fire burns low. An age that has made image-management a craft has only multiplied the servant-girls who see through it. “Be sure your sin will find you out” (Num 32:23).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honesty of the mouth: that speech is diagnostic, not decorative. Peter’s tongue bewrayed his fear; may ours bewray a better master. The man renewed by grace cannot wholly hide it either — the accent of the new birth clings to him, and his speech, seasoned with salt, discloses whose he is (Col 4:6).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Old English wrēgan, to accuse, comes a verb meaning to reveal or expose — near “betray” but not the same word.

expand to see more

Bewray — Middle English bewreyen; Old English wrēgan, to accuse.

It means to disclose or expose, not primarily to betray a trust.

Silence can bewray a man’s guilt as loudly as words (Pro 29:24).

Peter’s Galilean speech bewrayed him in the high priest’s hall (Mat 26:73).

What the heart hides, the mouth bewrays — the law of Matthew 12:34.

Usage

"His silence bewrayed him as surely as a confession would have."

"The heart’s abundance bewrays itself in the unguarded word."

"Grace, too, bewrays itself: the accent of heaven clings to the man."
